title: Your First Team: New Manager Guide to Delegation, Feedback, One-on-Ones, and Leading Forme
description: The promotion to manager is the hardest one in a career, because everything that earned it is suddenly the wrong job. Companies promote the best individual performer, hand them a team, and the skills invert overnight: the doing that got you here now competes with the leading the title requires. This is not your typical book series: this is a Coaching Session with your personal Leadership Coach, not a Sunday afternoon casual read. This book is the manual nobody hands the new manager: the identity shift from doing to enabling, the first conversations that set the ceiling, delegation as development rather than dumping, feedback that actually lands, the one-on-one rhythm that is the best management tool ever invented, and the trust your team decides to give you, or not, in about ninety days. Drills, scripts , worksheets , and a thirty-day plan included. Chad Pfeifer has spent twenty-five years developing managers, including as a Chief People Officer , and has watched month two drown a thousand stars. title: Leading Former Peers: A Practical Guide to Earning Trust, Setting Boundaries, and Managing
description: Getting promoted is exciting—until the people who once worked beside you begin looking to you for decisions, feedback, and accountability. Leading former peers creates challenges that ordinary management advice often overlooks. How do you preserve valuable relationships without showing favoritism? What should you say when a friend is underperforming? How can you establish authority without becoming distant, defensive, or controlling? Leading Former Peers offers a practical roadmap for making this difficult transition with clarity and confidence. Inside, readers will learn how to: Reset workplace relationships after promotion Establish authority without acting superior Create fair boundaries with workplace friends Address underperformance early and respectfully Handle resistance and public challenges Give clear, actionable feedback Manage ambitious or disappointed former peers Delegate without micromanaging Resolve conflict before teams divide into camps Lead meetings, decisions, and organizational change Build a focused thirty-sixty-ninety-day plan Each chapter combines practical guidance with realistic workplace scenarios, adaptable conversation language, reflection prompts, and immediate actions. The included manager’s toolkit provides reusable planners for one-to-one meetings, delegation, performance conversations, conflict resolution, decision-making, and weekly self-review. title: Leading Former Peers Without Losing Trust: How to Reset Relationships, Set Fair Boundaries
description: Getting promoted is exciting. Managing people who used to sit beside you is where the real transition begins. Leading Former Peers Without Losing Trust is a practical guide for professionals who have moved into management and now need to lead former coworkers, friends, or teammates. The work may be familiar, but the relationship has changed. Decisions carry more weight. Boundaries become visible. Feedback can feel personal. A choice that once felt casual can now affect trust across the team. This book focuses on the situations that make that transition difficult - and what to do about them. Inside, you will learn how to: • Reset the working relationship without becoming cold or distant • Set clear professional boundaries while keeping relationships human • Lead with authority without trying to prove that you deserve the promotion • Apply fair standards when friendships, history, or rivalries are involved • Delegate effectively when former teammates know the work better than you do • Give direct feedback without turning a work issue into a personal judgment • Handle pushback, disappointment, and public disagreement with steadiness • Navigate remote and hybrid communication when old informal channels continue • Use practical language for awkward conversations when you are not sure what to say • Build a simple rhythm for the first weeks and months in the new role You do not need to become a different person to become a manager. You need to recognize what changed, make expectations clear, and build a working relationship people can trust.  if(window.mix_csa){window.mix_csa('[cel_widget_id="tell-amazon-desktop_DetailPage_3"]', '#CardInstanceLqJPKXfH1QTfEgAViwRv5Q')('mark', 'bb')} if(window.uet){window.uet('bb','tell-amazon-desktop_DetailPage_3',{wb: 1})} ._tell-amazon-deskto

title: Leading Your Former Peers: A Practical First-30-Days Guide to Boundaries, Delegation, and
description: You got the promotion. Now you need to lead the people who used to work beside you. A familiar team can make a new management role harder to explain. A friend asks for an exception. An experienced colleague stays quiet. A task you thought was agreed remains unfinished. Leading Your Former Peers is a focused guide to preparing and following through on the conversations that come with managing former colleagues. Across eight chapters and 16 original fictional situations, you will find practical preparation, example dialogue, two alternative reactions for each situation, and a concrete follow-up. Use it to: • Clarify your responsibilities and decision-making authority with your manager. • Hold your first one-to-one meetings and reset working expectations. • Respond to friends' requests fairly and explain work boundaries. • Agree on tasks, give specific feedback, and address missed commitments. • Ask for support with repeated problems and review what to change after the first month. Read in order or use the linked conversation finder before a specific discussion. Short agendas, task agreements, and work-record examples are included in the text; no printing or separate download is required. Written for first-time managers with formal direct reports. The first 30 days organize the guide; they are not a promise of results within a month. description: Many people relish the opportunity to become a manager. Whether it's for status, progression, more money or more responsibility, moving into management often becomes the goal for progressive people. But what if you now have to lead the people who you were friends with, buddies, pals, people you drank with and played football with. Can the relationship ever be the same? description: Yesterday you were one of the team. Today you are responsible for leading it. An internal promotion changes the job before it changes the relationships. At the same time, you need to set priorities, delegate work, give feedback, handle conflict, and build a management rhythm that lasts beyond the first awkward weeks. Lead the Team You Came From gives first-time managers a practical 90-day operating system for making that transition without becoming distant, performative, or afraid to lead. Inside, you will learn how to: Reset former-peer relationships and clarify new boundaries Align authority and expectations with your own manager Run useful one-on-ones and team meetings Make priorities, decision rights, and follow-through visible Delegate outcomes without taking the work back Give fair, specific feedback when history is in the room Handle pushback, conflict, and early performance concerns Use Day 30, 60, and 90 checkpoints to see what is actually improving The book includes the Role Reset Map, First 10 Conversations Planner, Decision-Rights Map, Delegation Ladder, Fairness Audit, Weekly Manager Review, 30/60/90 Scorecard, Scenario Labs, and a quick-reference phrase bank. This is a practical management guide for people promoted from within their team, not an HR or employment-law manual. description: Yesterday you were on the team. Today you lead it. An internal promotion can feel like a win—and immediately create one of the hardest leadership transitions at work. title: From Peer to Manager: Practical Scripts for Your First 90 Days Leading Former Colleagues
description: Yesterday you were one of the team. Today you are the manager. A colleague who used to ask for your help now needs a decision. A friend expects the same easy access. It focuses on the decisions and conversations you are most likely to face, and gives you words to start them. Inside you will learn how to: Agree your remit with your own manager before making promises Hand off your previous duties cleanly instead of doing two jobs Have the transition conversations, including the awkward ones Keep friendships while making decisions fairly and transparently Use one-on-ones, delegate outcomes and give feedback former peers can use Respond to pushback, handle conflict and know when to escalate Manage up and make workload trade-offs visible Build a weekly rhythm the team can actually use Also included: a 90-day roadmap, a library of ready-to-adapt conversation scripts, and reusable worksheets. The scripts are starting points, not lines to memorize. Change the wording to fit your voice and your team. Keep the purpose: conversations that end with something usable, such as a decision, a clear boundary, a named owner or a date to revisit. title: Managing Friends & Former Peers: How to lead when the personal stakes are high–without des
description: Managing friends or former peers can be awkward. The moment you become the boss, everything changes. You are now accountable for the performance of people who used to be your friends or co-workers — and they must adjust to reporting to you. Everyone can feel hesitant, uncertain, and uncomfortable about what comes next. Some team members may: Feel they deserved the promotion you received Question whether you’re qualified Miss your predecessor and resent “starting over” Expect special treatment because of your past relationship Becoming a new leader is tough. Becoming the boss of friends or former peers can feel daunting. But it can be done. Managing Friends & Former Peers shows you exactly how to move forward with confidence, clarity, and professionalism—without damaging important relationships Like all Just in Time Leadership books, this one focuses on a single, critical leadership challenge: how to successfully manage people who used to be your equals. Along the way, you’ll strengthen essential management skills such as: Holding difficult conversations Setting clear expectations Coaching employees Establishing professional boundaries You won’t solve this by chance or by using a management “trick.” You’ll solve it by understanding what to do—and applying it immediately.
